title: Sessions offer advice on rising energy costs
summary: A council is urging people to seek support with rising energy costs on heating this winter.
text:
Sessions offer advice on rising energy costs
- Published
A charity is offering free advice on energy bills with prices expected to climb further from January.
Devon Communities Together said it was hosting drop-in sessions across the county, which include help with energy bills, smart meters and switching suppliers.
Gas and electricity bills for a typical household are forecast to rise by £443 a year from January. Heating oil prices have also risen drastically since the start of this year, from about 60p to £1.11 a litre, according to the Action with Communities in Rural England network.
Devon County Council said many households in rural parts relied on heating oil because they were not connected to mains gas.
Nora Corkery, chief executive of Devon Communities Together, said: "Behind every statistic is a household making difficult choices: rationing the heating, putting off filling up a tank, or cutting back on journeys they can't really do without."
The charity said people could access confidential one-to-one support to find financial help, with a limited number of free winter warm packs available for those who attend.
Cheryl Cottle-Hunkin, from Devon County Council, said: "I'd urge anyone who is struggling, or worried about the winter ahead, to seek advice and find out what help may be available."
More information on the sessions was available on the charity's website, external.

title: Opinion: When should medical school start?
summary: STAT readers weigh in on shortening medical school, fixing pediatric emergency care, and more.
text:
First Opinion is STAT’s platform for interesting, illuminating, and provocative articles about the life sciences writ large, written by biotech insiders, health care workers, researchers, and others.
To encourage robust, good-faith discussion about issues raised in First Opinion essays, STAT publishes selected Letters to the Editor received in response to them. You can submit a Letter to the Editor here, or find the submission form at the end of any First Opinion essay.
The story
“Medical school should start after students take the Step 1 exam,” by Rachel E. Fabi and Amy Caruso Brown
The response
The authors’ proposal hinges on the premise that learning the foundational sciences and learning to become a physician can be separated without compromising either. My first year of medical school was peppered with clinical exposure and taught me otherwise. I floundered with a blood pressure cuff during a wellness visit, fumbled for words as I interviewed a man waiting for a heart transplant, and listened to a patient recount her immense sorrow after multiple miscarriages. These encounters remain among my most formative.
I agree with the authors that students are often preoccupied with medical licensure exams, and that early clinical exposure might not cure this. In my experience, however, it is the strongest counterweight. After meeting those patients, I was learning for more than an exam. The proposed model would abandon that counterweight. Students would still encounter patients eventually, but we would have forfeited valuable time. Becoming a compassionate, humanistic physician is slow work, and it deserves all the time we can offer. A flashcard can teach a student what causes a miscarriage. It takes a patient to teach what it means to grieve one. And that lesson should not wait until after Step 1.
— Surya Pulukuri, Harvard Medical School student
The story
“The economics of the U.S. health care system are broken,” by Paul Markovich
The response
Markovich is correct: The U.S. health care “non-system” is broken. There are many culprits, including hospitals, whose prices are set more by market dominance than by quality. He should also look at the administrative complexity driven largely by our myriad of private insurance companies. Some 25% of U.S. “health care” spending goes to administrative costs. The insurers need to agree on a single set of billing codes and procedures to cut doctors’ and hospitals’ cost of billing. They need to sit down with doctors and come up with a uniform set of procedures needing pre-authorization and a single set of criteria. They need to agree on a small number of policy options that are understandable to the public. Finger-pointing is easy, but should start at home.
— Edward Hoffer, M.D., Harvard Medical School

title: Anthropic says it will put humanity first. Will its IPO change that?
summary: Critics say now that the AI giant is a public company, its commitment to put safety ahead of commercial success will be tested.
text:
Anthropic says it will put humanity first. Will its IPO change that?
As Anthropic executives and co-founders gathered to celebrate the artificial intelligence company's market debut at the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday, CEO Dario Amodei spoke about AI's potential benefits, and risks, to humanity.
"There is a gigantic difference between how AI will go if we pay little attention to safety versus how it will go if we are obsessed with safety," Amodei said before ringing the ceremonial opening bell. "And an obsession with safety and public benefit has been built into Anthropic's DNA from the start."
Anthropic raised a record $81.3 billion from the IPO and a further $26 billion through a separate private placement, surpassing SpaceX and vaulting into the ranks of publicly traded companies worth more than $1 trillion.
The company has built its reputation on the promise that developing safe AI matters more than winning the race for commercial dominance. It has cultivated an image as an AI safety pioneer, presenting itself as a company willing to put humanity's long-term interests ahead of industry competition.
But now that Anthropic is a public company, that commitment faces a new test. The IPO has brought in new investors, greater scrutiny and pressure to deliver returns to shareholders. Some critics question whether the company can stay true to its founding mission.
The commercial demands of being a public company may cloud safety decisions that could negatively impact the company's share price, such as delaying the release of potentially risky models, legal experts told NPR.
Anthropic's concerns about AI safety are not merely part of its public messaging. Amodei has repeatedly warned about the potential threats advanced AI models pose to humanity, particularly if they escape the control of their developers. The company's IPO prospectus echoed those concerns, warning that "sufficiently advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to society if not developed and deployed responsibly."
Anthropic also acknowledged that it may ultimately lose control of its own models.
"There can be no assurance, however, that the safeguards or access regimes we adopt will prove adequate, that we will correctly identify which capabilities require restriction, or that constraints we impose will not be circumvented," the company warned investors.
Anthropic's founders and employees just got very rich
Anthropic's corporate structure is intended to protect its mission, even as it pursues commercial success. Anthropic is a public benefit corporation (PBC), meaning its board must balance shareholder interests with its social mission.
As part of that structure, the company has installed an oversight body known as the Long-Term Benefit Trust, which has the power to appoint four of the company's seven directors. The founders effectively control the appointment of the remaining three.

title: GTA 6 sales hit $3.8bn in a single day - the biggest entertainment launch in history
summary: The mammoth figure surpasses every video game launch and single-day film box office record.
text:
GTA 6 sales hit $3.8bn in a single day - the biggest entertainment launch in history
- Published
Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6) saw record retail sales in its first full-day of release, hitting $3.8bn (£2.9bn), making it the biggest entertainment launch in history.
Take-Two, the parent company of Rockstar Games, said on Friday the figures were based on estimates through end of day on Thursday and marked a record for "entertainment across any medium". It pre-sold 32.5m copies of the game.
To compare, Spider-Man: Brand New Day, this year's highest-grossing film so far, made $2.5bn (£1.8bn) over its entire run in cinemas.
Internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare said earlier that PS5 downloads in the UK peaked at 8.6 times normal levels around its launch.
New Zealand, where GTA 6 was first available, saw a 14.8-fold spike four hours before, suggesting some players switched regions for early access.
In its initial findings since the game's launch, Cloudflare also recorded a huge surge in traffic to Rockstar's online services, peaking at 11.2 times normal levels in Australia and 9.3 times on the US East Coast.
In Europe, UK interest was particularly strong, reaching seven times normal levels compared with 5.3 times in France and Germany.
The record smashes that of its predecessor - from 13 years prior - Grand Theft Auto V. The game previously held the best opening week sales in video-game history, earning $1.15bn (£1.2bn) in just five days.
The game is the latest instalment in Rockstar's nearly three decade old crime simulator franchise, which has become one of the most popular games in history.
At its core, the series is a satirical take on the American dream, putting players in the shoes of career criminals in Leonida, the game's Florida-inspired state.
The latest release follows new characters, a pair of small-time criminals Lucia and her partner Jason.
GTA 6 is estimated to have cost more than $1bn to develop, which would make it the most expensive video game in history.
Research firm Sensor Tower said GTA 6 will be so popular that it will reduce the time gamers spend on other single-player titles by 10%.
The firm said its estimates are based on email receipts data and other statistical sources that track millions of people daily. They also track public profiles across major gaming platforms like PlayStation and Xbox, where GTA 6 is available.
Around three quarters of the game's sales have been on PlayStation 5 and the balance on Xbox, Sensor Tower said.
Niko Partners, a gaming market research firm, said it expects GTA 6 to make more than $3bn in sales worldwide this year.
That figure would rank GTA 6 among the highest-grossing entertainment releases ever, but it would still have some way to go to catch 1939's Gone with the Wind, which has made an estimated $4.5bn (£3.44bn), adjusted for inflation.
Rockstar is expected to make even more money from GTA 6 over the coming years.
The New York-based studio has yet to announce when the game will be released

title: Opinion: How Kennedy and MAHA could help stop measles
summary: Kennedy and MAHA say they aren’t anti-vaccine. They can prove it by promoting the MMR vaccine, writes Brinda Adhikari.
text:
A version of this article first appeared on the Substack of “Why Should I Trust You?”
On Tuesday, after the United States lost its measles elimination status, health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. posted on X that he wanted to stop measles from spreading in America. “We will stop measles outbreaks, protect American families, and work to regain U.S. measles elimination status. I continue to recommend [measles, mumps, and rubella] vaccination as the most effective way to prevent measles.”
Well, Secretary Kennedy, do I have an idea for you …
It involves mobilizing a movement you helped build, a movement that has successfully organized millions of Americans around issues related to their health. I’m talking about MAHA.
Right now, the discourse is playing out like this: Medical societies are expressing alarm over the loss of measles elimination status, while many politicians blame Kennedy and the Trump administration for failing to adequately respond.
Kennedy’s defenders clap back by reminding us that other countries have lost elimination status in recent years, too, that these are all efforts to undermine Kennedy and that his administration is doing what it can.
I understand on some level that, as a society, we need to litigate what went wrong. But candidly, I’m much more interested in something else: Who might be best positioned to reach the Americans that public health officials are struggling to persuade to get the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine?
What I learned from listening
I’ll start by saying that I believe in the measles vaccine. I was vaccinated as a child. I’ve vaccinated my two kids. I don’t identify as particularly vaccine skeptical. I’ve sometimes wondered why we have so many vaccine recommendations in this country compared with others, but I generally trust my doctors and haven’t (yet) experienced any major adverse reactions that might have led me to question that trust.
Over the last two years of making the podcast “Why Should I Trust You?,” my co-hosts and I have had the privilege of speaking with many people who feel quite differently than I do about vaccines, public health, and the medical system, and what they see as blind faith in expertise.
I’ve learned a tremendous amount. These conversations have made me question my own assumptions and better understand why I trust institutions, while sometimes realizing that I, too, harbor mistrust. While some of these conversations have been with people who are unwaveringly anti-vaccine, most have been with people who have taken some vaccines and harbor doubts about others.

title: The AI boom had a really bad week — and it's raising loud alarms
summary: AI stocks — and the broader markets — got pummeled this week, raising major concerns about the financial system and the wider economy. Here's what to know.
text:
The AI boom had a really bad week — and it's raising loud alarms
A yearslong AI boom showed signs of unraveling this week in spectacular fashion.
AI-related stocks have powered markets to record highs and helped support the broader economy. But investors now fear that a potential bubble in the sector could be bursting, which could spark wider financial repercussions.
Here's what to know about the week in AI and why alarm bells are ringing
What happened with stock markets this week?
Investors were hoping the stock market debut of AI giant Anthropic this week would provide a boost to the markets. Instead, the entire stock market got pummeled on Friday, sparking one of the worst weeks that Wall Street has seen in quite some time.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped 10% for the week, its worst performance since the onset of COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns in March 2020. Even Anthropic, which gained 17% on its debut, ended up slumping more than 8% to close near its IPO price on Friday.
Meanwhile, both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average entered a correction as of the close of trade on Friday, meaning a drop of 10% from their recent highs.
What's behind the steep drops?
It's the culmination of weeks of fears that have been building up about the sustainability of the AI trade.
Back in September, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in over three years. That poses a big challenge to AI companies because they still need to borrow billions of dollars to do things like build out data centers that power the growth of their technologies. Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for them.
Democrats also took over both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, vowing to take a tougher regulatory approach toward the AI sector and slow down the build-out of data centers, which have been unpopular with voters.
Democrats were also elected as governors in states that have been key to the data center build-out, like Texas, where Gina Hinojosa stunned the political world by winning her race.
And then there's the turmoil at Nvidia, the top AI chip company. Its CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned this month after being suspected of having had an affair with a woman who's believed to have been spying for China.
All this has exacerbated investors' worries about the sustainability of an AI trade into which investors have sunk billions of dollars.
Hank Smith, the head of investment strategy at Haverford Trust, thinks it's unlikely the markets will recover quickly, the way they have previously bounced right back after AI shares dropped.
"I think it has taken the market the better part of the last two or three weeks to realize it is not going to be like the previous sell-offs," Smith said, adding that AI could fall "out of favor" through next year.
"It's just going to take a little bit of time to heal," he said of the tech market.

title: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
summary: Pressures weighed on US markets, with the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average pushed into correction territory.
text:
Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
- Published
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.
The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors.
Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week.
Both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.
The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago.
The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.
Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development.
Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday.
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.
Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.
Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.
Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.
While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.
"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.
"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."

title: ICE detention of Princeton scientist rattles academia
summary: A graduate student who is a scientific researcher at Princeton was detained by ICE while traveling home after presenting at a neuroscience conference.
text:
A graduate student who is a scientific researcher at Princeton University was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement earlier this week while traveling home after presenting research at the annual Society for Neuroscience conference in Washington, D.C.
The researcher, Eva Yi Xie, was detained Thursday. Although she has lived in the U.S. since 2016 after moving to the country from China, her visa had expired, according to The New York Times. Her lawyers told a reporter Xie had a pending asylum application and was thus allowed to remain in the country legally.
The news, first posted by a mentor of Xie’s on X, ricocheted across academic circles on Friday, in part because it seemed to crystalize pervasive fears of non-U.S. academics and international students that traveling to conferences to present new research and network with colleagues may be too risky during a second Trump administration that has cracked down on immigration.
“There’s, I think, an open question about whether or not it’s safe for people who are international students on visas to travel, because there have been these detentions, and that’s a very scary prospect,” said Caitlin Rivers, a John Hopkins academic who said a staff member of hers was detained by ICE earlier this year. A number of U.S. conferences have reported smaller attendance over the past two years, and some have considered hosting in other countries.
ICE did not respond to a request for comment as to why Xie was detained. But the administration has been vocal in its desire to reduce the number of foreign-born graduate students in the U.S. In its science blueprint released earlier this year, the White House wrote “America’s over-reliance on foreign students also creates a security challenge.”
Xie is not the first graduate student to be detained. In one notable instance, Tufts researcher Rumeysa Ozturk was detained by ICE last year in Cambridge, Mass., and later decided to leave the country. A report released earlier this week found that international graduate student enrollment is down by a third at academic medical centers.
“News of Eva’s detention is distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community,” Rodney D. Priestley, the dean of Princeton University’s graduate school, wrote in a statement, adding the university has provided Xie with legal representation. “We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton.”
Xie’s work lies at the intersection of neuroscience and artificial intelligence; she uses a combination of experiments on mice and large datasets of neural recordings to understand how different portions of the brain work together to make decisions. A third-year PhD student, she is viewed as a rising star by some of her colleagues.

title: Trump's impact on an Ohio steel plant
summary: The giant steel plant in Middletown, Ohio planned to switch away from using coke, a refined form of coal. The switch would have cut hazardous air pollution -- and greenhouse gas emissions. But that plan has changed under President Trump
text:
Trump's impact on an Ohio steel plant
The giant steel plant in Middletown, Ohio planned to switch away from using coke, a refined form of coal. The switch would have cut hazardous air pollution — and greenhouse gas emissions. But that plan has changed under President Trump
AILSA CHANG, HOST:
In Middletown, Ohio, a big steel mill is the city's largest employer and the biggest source of local air pollution. Under the Biden administration, the mill had planned to clean up its operations by shifting away from coal, but that has changed under President Trump. Middletown is now one example of the administration's efforts to boost fossil fuels. The Allegheny Front's Reid Frazier reports.
REID FRAZIER, BYLINE: Donna Ballinger stands outside her house in Middletown, Ohio.
(SOUNDBITE OF HORN HONKING)
FRAZIER: Through a thicket of trees, she points to the Middletown Works, a steel mill which rises several stories above her home.
DONNA BALLINGER: And it runs 24/7. You don't get a break.
FRAZIER: The plant makes steel the traditional way - using coke, a refined form of coal. That process emits a lot of air pollution, including carbon dioxide, which contributes to climate change. It also releases lots of soot, which drifts down onto Ballinger's neighborhood.
BALLINGER: It's the fallout that's on everything we own, cars, property, kids' toys. You can't touch anything. You can't open your windows.
FRAZIER: That soot is bad for human health. According to the EPA, the tiny particles are linked to higher rates of heart and lung problems, including asthma. Ballinger eventually got so fed up with the air quality, she began working with the local Sierra Club to try to force the plant to clean up.
Then a few years ago, the steel mill did announce plans to cut its air pollution. Its owner, Cleveland-Cliffs, said it would convert to a new steelmaking process that doesn't use coal. Instead, it would switch to using natural gas or hydrogen. That would cut both the plant's local air pollution and its carbon footprint. That's important because the steel industry is a major source of climate pollution. CEO Lourenco Goncalves told investors at the time, hydrogen was the solution.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
LAURENCO GONCALVES: We believe hydrogen will be the true game changer for the decarbonization of steel.
FRAZIER: The Biden administration agreed. It awarded the Middletown Steel Mill $500 million as part of its climate agenda. But then Donald Trump came into office promising to boost fossil fuels like coal. Soon after, Goncalvez told investors the hydrogen project was off. Middletown is also the hometown of a major figure in the Trump administration.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
JD VANCE: It is great to be home. It is great to be back in Middletown, Ohio.

title: UK to explore even closer ties with EU after agreeing deal, says Burnham
summary: The UK-EU deal agreed on Friday covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
text:
UK to explore even closer ties with EU after agreeing deal, says Burnham
- Published
Andy Burnham said the UK will discuss possible options for even closer ties with the EU, after agreeing a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
The prime minister said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, adding the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year.
European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".
Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week.
Burnham arrived in Brussels to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU, which originally began under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.
The agreements announced on Friday included scrapping most of the checks on British food exports, in return for the UK following some EU regulations, from 2028.
The UK government believes the changes will cut costs for businesses and could bring prices down for shoppers, while critics argue the change will make the UK a "rule taker" from Brussels rather than a rule maker.
The new youth experience scheme will allow up to 100,000 18 to 31 year olds from the EU to travel, work and study in the UK for up to three years. The same number of young Britons will be allowed into Europe.
The two sides want to ensure that opportunities under the annual scheme will be available to young people by no later than January 2030.
A further six months is available to discuss a deal on tuition fees, which could prove to be a potential stumbling block.

title: What’s Behind a Recent Spike in Early Social Security Claims?
summary: Experts point to well-publicized turmoil at the Social Security Administration last year as a potential spark.
text:
Until recently, economic researchers were cheering an encouraging trend: Older Americans were staying in the labor force longer and waiting longer to claim their Social Security benefits, aiming to enhance their financial stability in retirement.
Not everyone, of course. Despite financial advisers’ counsel and economists’ hopes, most people still claim their benefits before reaching their designated full retirement age, though that usually means lower monthly payments for life.
Early claimers might hit an unexpected financial crunch, as Alan Turner did when he lost his job as a museum exhibit designer in 2022. “I haphazardly looked for work, but my prospects weren’t very good,” he said.
For a while, Turner, 69, who lives in New Castle, Delaware, got by on unemployment benefits and savings, hoping to reach his full retirement age — 66 and a half — before claiming. “It was doable, but it was bleak,” he said. He took his benefits at 64, reducing his Social Security income by about $5,000 a year.
Or people might feel the need to retire earlier than planned. Nancy Mansson, a nuclear medicine technologist in West Hebron, New York, found last year that “I was just fried,” she said. “I had to step away,” though she was more than a year short of her full retirement age.
People can claim Social Security retirement benefits as early as 62, but their payments will be substantially lower than if they wait until full retirement age, now 67 for those born in 1960 or later.
Mansson, 67, sacrificed about $300 a month by claiming early and works at a hospital one day a week to compensate.
Still, economists had documented that Americans were both retiring later and claiming their benefits later — until last year, when “all hell broke loose,” said Alicia Munnell, former director of the Center for Retirement Research at Boston College. In an unprecedented surge, hundreds of thousands more people than usual suddenly filed for retirement benefits.
Why? Understanding what’s happening with older Americans and Social Security requires looking both backward and ahead.
For decades, workers had been retiring at increasingly younger ages; that trend reversed in the 1980s, and the change accelerated in the 1990s. Changes in the Social Security law, which Congress amended in 1983 (“The last time we did anything to Social Security,” Munnell said, pointedly) provided incentives to work longer.
Most employers shifted from defined pensions to 401(k) plans and discontinued retiree health insurance, additional reasons to stay on the job. Plus, work had become less physically demanding overall, and “health and longevity were increasing,” Munnell said.
In an analysis the center published last year, the proportion of men who were filing at 62 fell to 26% in 2023 from 31% in 2019; among women, claiming at 62 dropped to 27% from 34%. Over the same period, claiming at 67 or later rose to 26% from 19% for men and to 25% from 20% for women, a trend that persisted into 2024.

title: Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow
summary: The trade deal is unlikely lower food prices for shoppers, but should boost the economy more than other post-Brexit agreements.
text:
Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow
- Published
The prime minister made a lot of the UK's new deal with the EU cutting costs for business and consumers during tough times.
In another world, Andy Burnham would have loved for the nation's supermarkets to clearly announce that they could cut food prices as a result of this latest agreement on food exports.
And while grocers have very much welcomed Friday's announcement, they have notably not committed to price cuts as a direct result of this move.
The managing director of M&S, Alex Freudmann, called the deal a "major step forward", saying it would remove bureaucracy. Tesco chief executive Ken Murphy added it was "good news for British farmers and producers".
Freudmann highlighted some of hoops that were hurting UK-EU trade, using the example that "getting our spaghetti Bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet's signature and even the Latin name of a cow".
Such measures will no longer need to be taken once this deal kicks in. Good news for business exports then, but will that lead to lower shopping bills here in the UK?
This deal will matter for food exporters - it may not have a clear visible impact at the checkout.
Privately, industry insiders say there are too many moving parts in the world economy, especially given the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.
It is more a hope than will at this stage. The industry and government hope that the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers.
This is not the first time Labour has sought to reduce the weekly shop costs. Sir Keir Starmer's administration floated the idea that supermarkets might even offer some form of branded discounts, a suggestion that was met with collective bemusement by those in the industry.
However, there will be less paperwork, checks and red tape on food imports too, but they were already lightly enforced.
No longer will hundreds of pages of documents be required. No longer will perishable goods lose valuable hours or days at border checks. No longer will the incorrect colour of ink or Latin name for a meat disallow a shipment of British exports.
Some, though not all of the 24% hit since 2019 to the real value of agrifood exports, could be regained by a bonfire of this red tape.
In particular, smaller exporters of food will be able to return to the large EU market.
But the extra benefit here is unclear, and there could be extra checks and costs required instead on non-EU food imports.
The government's own assessment is that the economy will gain £5bn through this, or 0.14% by 2040.
Critics point out that this benefit does not include the quid pro quo - having to align with EU laws. Farmers have pointed to compliance with pesticides and fungicide regulation.

summary: Anthropic's initial public offering was a success for shareholders, including its founders. But there were also protests about whether the company can be a responsible steward of AI technology.
text:
Critics are worried about Anthropic's influence after first day of public trading
Anthropic's initial public offering was a success for shareholders, including its founders. But there were also protests about whether the company can be a responsible steward of AI technology.
STEVE INSKEEP, HOST:
Anthropic is now worth $2 trillion, judging by its stock price. The company behind Claude held its initial public offering. It now has a lot of funding to balance the many critics of AI. NPR's Shannon Bond reports.
SHANNON BOND, BYLINE: Inside the Nasdaq stock exchange, Anthropic's executives and co-founders rang the ceremonial bell to open trading on Thursday morning.
(SOUNDBITE OF BELL RINGING)
BOND: Outside in Times Square, a small group of protesters chanted.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
UNIDENTIFIED PROTESTERS: (Chanting) Why you doing IPO? This AI bubble about to blow.
BOND: Activists and AI safety researchers also gathered outside Anthropic's headquarters in downtown San Francisco. They called on the company to slow down the development of advanced AI.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
UNIDENTIFIED ACTIVISTS #1: (Chanting) Please do not accelerate.
UNIDENTIFIED ACTIVISTS #2: (Chanting) Just ask the state to regulate.
BOND: A handful of protesters were arrested in both cities. Anthropic is the first company purely focused on artificial intelligence to go public. And the IPO comes as debates are raging around AI, from the impact of data centers to fears of job losses to worries about AI going rogue. Anthropic itself has fueled some of those fears. It was founded five years ago by a breakaway group of OpenAI employees who were worried that the company wasn't taking safety seriously enough. Before ringing the Nasdaq bell on Thursday, CEO Dario Amodei said Anthropic remains committed to keeping the technology under human control. He said the company won't bend to business or political pressure.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
DARIO AMODEI: If we can show it's possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same. We call this a race to the top.
BOND: Amodei and his six co-founders each made about $280 million selling shares in this week's IPO. They each hold a stake in the company worth about $23 billion at Thursday's closing price.
Shannon Bond, NPR News.
INSKEEP: And we'll note that Anthropic is a financial supporter of NPR.

title: Ahead of Thanksgiving, Readers Show Grace and Grit
summary: KFF Health News gives readers a chance to comment on a recent batch of stories.
text:
Letters to the Editor is a periodic feature. We welcome all comments and will publish a selection. We edit for length and clarity and require full names.
Reader Recipe Exchange
Just saw Rachana Pradhan’s Nov. 13 “The Week in Brief” newsletter (“He Was Diagnosed With Cancer. Then His Medicaid Was Thrown Into Question”). Nice reporting out of Nebraska! Tongue-in-cheek, she asked for Thanksgiving Day recipe submissions. So, below is my recipe for roasted carrots and green sauce. A tasty, veggie-forward side:
Roasted Rainbow Carrots with Green Sauce
Ingredients
For the carrots:
- Rainbow carrots, with about 1 inch of green tops left attached
- Extra-virgin olive oil, for coating
- Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper
For the green sauce:
- 1 small bunch cilantro, tough stems trimmed
- 1 small bunch parsley, tough stems trimmed
- 3 oil-packed anchovy fillets
- 1 small garlic clove, crushed
- ⅔ cup extra-virgin olive oil
- 5 Tbs. fresh lemon juice
- 2 tsps. Dijon mustard
- Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper, to taste
Instructions
- Prepare the oven and carrots. Heat the oven to 425°F. Line a rimmed sheet pan with parchment paper. Trim the carrot greens, leaving about 1 inch attached. I like keeping this little bit of green because it crisps up deliciously in the oven. Scrub the carrots, leaving the skins on, and wash carefully around the tops. Pat dry. Halve any thick carrots lengthwise so they cook evenly.
- Season and roast. Place the carrots on the prepared pan. Drizzle with olive oil, lightly coating the attached greens as well. Sprinkle with salt and pepper. Toss to coat. Arrange in a single layer with space between them. Roast for 20–30 minutes, turning halfway through, until deeply caramelized and fork-tender. Larger carrots may need additional time.
- Make the green sauce. Combine the cilantro, parsley, anchovies, garlic, olive oil, lemon juice, and Dijon mustard in a blender or food processor. Purée until nearly smooth. Taste and season with salt and pepper, keeping in mind that the anchovies already add salt.
- Serve. Transfer the warm carrots to a serving platter and spoon some of the green sauce over them, leaving the crisp tops exposed. Serve the remaining sauce on the side.
— Andy DiAntonio, director of communications for the National Health Law Program; Washington, D.C.

title: How exactly did Trump get so rich on crypto? We explain
summary: President Trump has made billions of dollars in his second term — most of it in cryptocurrencies. Democrats are vowing to probe his businesses as they gear up to take over Congress next year.
text:
How exactly did Trump get so rich on crypto? We explain
Trump's crypto profits raise alarms for transparency advocates
For the last year, Will Ragland and a team of researchers at the Center for American Progress — a left-leaning think tank in Washington, D.C. — have dedicated themselves to counting how much money President Trump and his family have made in his second term.
So far, they put the total at nearly $3 billion. More than 2 billion dollars of the earnings come from cryptocurrency ventures.
"You could probably combine all of the past presidents' income made during their time in office," Ragland says. "And it wouldn't come close to what we're seeing here."
This unprecedented profit could soon become a major political problem for the president.
After campaigning heavily on an anti-corruption message that resonated with voters, Democrats are promising to make holding Trump and his administration accountable a critical plank of their oversight agenda when they take over both the Senate and the House next year.
From Sen. Elizabeth Warren from Massachusetts to Rep. Robert Garcia from California, prominent Democrats are vowing to hold oversight hearings and hold President Trump and his administration accountable.
"Americans should be secure in the knowledge that their government is focused on their best interests—not on making the President's family richer," Rep. Garcia warned in a letter after the midterms this month warning Trump, his family and his administration to preserve records.
Here's a guide to how Trump made his crypto wealth.
Trump's meme coin
Shortly before his inauguration in early 2025, Trump and now-First Lady Melania Trump each launched their own meme coins — or cryptocurrencies based on Internet memes, cartoon characters, or even jokes.
Trump made over $600 million from the meme coin called $TRUMP, according to the president's own disclosures.
In an effort to drum up demand for the coin, Trump also held two galas for the top holders of $TRUMP. The president promised the closest access to himself to those who invested the most in the coin.
A third gala is scheduled for Sunday at his golf course in Virginia.
Many of the guests for the first event last year were likely to have been foreign, according to media reports. The second dinner, held this year, attracted considerably less interest, though participants also described a significant presence of people from abroad.
For Ragland and other anti-corruption activists, the dinners raise significant concerns about potential conflicts of interest.
"This is a way for foreign investors, foreign countries in some instances, to try and get as much influence as they can and use that as leverage for deals that they want to make that are helpful to them," Ragland says.
Already, top Democrats including Rep. Jamie Raskin from Maryland have launched investigations — and the galas are likely to become an aspect of their oversight into Trump's crypto ventures next year.

title: Airbnb's divisive new house rules come into force
summary: New rules on what Airbnb hosts can reasonably ask guests to do could mean fewer chores but higher costs for customers.
text:
Airbnb's divisive new house rules come into force
- Published
New rules on what Airbnb hosts can reasonably ask guests to do have come into force.
Hosts should now not normally ask guests to wash up, for example, but can appeal to Airbnb if they have a compelling reason.
Some guests have found lists of house rules laborious to complete, with one telling the BBC "it was not relaxing at all".
But some hosts have said that the costs of paying for extra cleaning may have to be passed on to customers.
The new Airbnb rules, announced last month, allow hosts to choose from seven standard house rules, which include determining how many people can stay overnight, and whether or not pets or smoking are allowed.
Hosts can then set additional rules, but guests shouldn't be asked to do the washing up, remove sheets from beds, take rubbish out or avoid using utilities.
Airbnb has begun reviewing listings and will be sending emails to hosts, external "who need to take action" it said.
Hosts can appeal to Airbnb to argue an additional house rule is necessary, and ask Airbnb to approve it.
If the house rule is not approved and the host keeps it anyway, Airbnb will flag this to guests on the host's listing page with a message such as "includes cleaning tasks".
Airbnb said chores can make customers hesitate about booking through the platform, arguing that making house rules "clearer" would increase the number of clients.
But some hosts have said they may have to pass the extra cleaning costs on to guests.
Lisa Clewes, who runs a Welsh holiday let, told the BBC she was "horrified" at the state her guests left the house after a dinner party.
There were broken glasses, drinks cans on the floor, pans full of food on the table and fish guts left in the garden.
Clewes said it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her three-bedroom property.
She said guests leaving more mess could mean hiring extra cleaners and increasing costs – expenses that may ultimately be passed on to her customers.
Edinburgh-based holiday home owner Fiona Venter told the BBC that Airbnb's new rules were "nonsense" and would not accept bookings if guests refuse to take their rubbish away.
Talking about a time when she was worried she might get a mice infestation after six bags of rubbish were left in her cottage, she said: "I would rather have my house still standing."
But Fiona said increased cleaning costs due to the rule change would be unfair to those who do clean up after themselves: "Why should they pay extra for the guests that choose to abuse a cottage?"
The changes have come as a relief to guests like Jessica Newhook, who says she has been faced with lengthy checkout lists, often on top of hefty cleaning fees.
She booked an Airbnb in Florida for a family reunion of 11 guests and says they had to "leave the property move-in ready for the cleaners", despite paying a $250 (£187) cleaning fee.
"We had rules about everything and it was not relaxing at all," she said.
The new rules h
